text: Lesson 18 introduced Workflow state as a field on kb_knowledge. Three of its values form the publishing path every article actually walks through on its way to being visible to end users.

Draft is while an author is still writing or editing, not visible to end users. Review is once the author considers it finished and submits it for sign-off. Published is once it has cleared that review and is now visible to whoever that Knowledge Base's permissions allow. A fourth value, Retired, covers an article's life after it stops being current — that's next lesson's subject.

It's tempting to treat the approval step as red tape slowing down a helpful author. The real reason it exists is scale. One author's draft, published straight to the Self-Service Knowledge Base with no second set of eyes, might contain a step that's subtly wrong or guidance that's simply out of date. Multiply that across hundreds of articles and thousands of readers, and an inaccurate article doesn't just mislead one person — it spreads bad guidance at scale, with other agents citing it as fact. The approval gate is what catches that before it goes live, not after.

Flow Designer and Platform Automation covered building an approval into any record flow, and Knowledge Management reuses that exact mechanism. A flow triggers when a kb_knowledge record's Workflow state changes to Review, and its action is Ask for Approval, routed to a Knowledge manager or a subject-matter expert for that Knowledge Base's Category. On approval, the flow sets Workflow state to Published and stamps a Published date. There's no path from Draft straight to Published that skips this flow.

A reviewer who finds a problem doesn't just leave a comment and move on. Rejecting the approval record routes the flow back to setting Workflow state to Draft, with the reviewer's comments attached to the record for the original author to act on. The article never reaches end users in its flawed form — it simply returns to Draft, now with specific feedback instead of a silent rejection.

Draft, Review, Published, and a real approval gate enforced through Flow Designer. Next up: what happens after Published — the real feedback mechanism end users have, and why retiring an outdated article is not the same thing as deleting it.
